blocks.text: Tarek Atoui’s entrancing Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern is an interconnected musical machine you can lose yourself in for hours. The artist teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear – managing to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. Read the five-star review .

blocks.alt: Albert Cornelis and Associates The Virgin and Child in a Landscape
blocks.caption: Photograph: © The National Gallery, London.

blocks.text: The Virgin and Child in a Landscape, 1520s, by Albert Cornelis and Associates Behind the melancholic Madonna and lively Christ child in this Renaissance painting is a fantasy version of the city of Bruges in a blue landscape that is nothing like the Flemish city’s actual setting. The city’s towers are depictions of the real towers of Bruges, the medieval powerhouse of industry and commerce where Albert Cornelis worked. But he or a helper have turned Bruges into a twinkling, dreamlike place beside a vast, placid sea inlet, loomed over by huge mountains: an imagined, alluring landscape inspired by the science-fiction utopias of Hieronymus Bosch, as well as the surreal vistas of Joachim Patinir. It may even owe something to the melting blue mountains and seas in Leonardo da Vinci’s altarpieces, for this painting was apparently made for the Italian market and has the name of an early Italian owner on the back. It’s a lovely, little known example of the way 16th-century artists could combine religious imagery with romantic, bizarre musings in their freely painted landscapes. National Gallery, London
